title: 1.4–1.6 Catch-Up
contentObjective: I can show I am caught up on Lessons 1.4–1.6 by using each lesson's big idea in mixed practice.
languageObjective: I can explain which lesson's big idea I used and how, using key vocabulary from Lessons 1.4–1.6.

vocabulary.definition: A chain of reasons — equations, drawings, or words — used to defend your thinking.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Una cadena de razones — ecuaciones, dibujos o palabras — que usas para defender tu pensamiento.
vocabulary.example: I recommend two jumbo boxes because their total volume is greater.

vocabulary.definition: A mathematical statement you believe is true but have not yet proven.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Una afirmación matemática que crees verdadera pero que aún no has probado.
vocabulary.example: I think the two jumbo boxes hold more cereal than the three large boxes.

vocabulary.definition: Something that repeats or changes in a predictable way.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Algo que se repite o cambia de una manera predecible.
vocabulary.example: The value of each type of coin is a pattern: 100 pennies make $1.00, 100 nickels make $5.00.

vocabulary.definition: The instruction that tells how to get from one number in a pattern to the next.
vocabulary.definitionEs: La instrucción que dice cómo pasar de un número del patrón al siguiente.
vocabulary.example: Player A's pattern rule is to add 2 after every made shot.

vocabulary.definition: To figure out what a problem is asking — what you know, and what you don't know yet.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Descubrir qué pide un problema: qué sabes y qué no sabes todavía.
vocabulary.example: Before computing, I ask: what is this problem really asking me to find?

vocabulary.definition: A way of showing a problem — a drawing, table, equation, or model — that helps you see it.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Una forma de mostrar un problema — un dibujo, una tabla, una ecuación o un modelo — que te ayuda a verlo.
vocabulary.example: Drawing the bicycle rack instead of only imagining it.

launch.narrative: Missed a lesson — or just want a refresher? This catch-up station reviews Lessons 1.4–1.6: 1.4 Math is Explaining and Sharing, 1.5 Math is Finding Patterns, 1.6 Math is Ours. Read the Big Ideas, warm up with the review problem, then prove you're caught up in the mixed practice.

conceptIntro.heading: The Big Ideas — Lessons 1.4–1.6
conceptIntro.intro: Here is the one thing to remember from each lesson, plus a quick guided example. If one of these feels shaky, that lesson is right above this one in the menu — you can open it any time.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: 1.4: We can defend a recommendation using equations, drawings, or words — and volume in cubic units gives the equations something exact to say. • 1.5: We use the patterns and relationships we notice to solve problems, make generalizations, and check that our solutions are reasonable. • 1.6: We make sense of problems, look for patterns, choose representations and tools, make a plan, watch our progress, and shift strategies when needed — together and on our own.

iDo.title: The Big Ideas (one per lesson)
lines: Lesson 1.4 — Math is Explaining and Sharing: We can defend a recommendation using equations, drawings, or words — and volume in cubic units gives the equations something exact to say.
Lesson 1.5 — Math is Finding Patterns: We use the patterns and relationships we notice to solve problems, make generalizations, and check that our solutions are reasonable.
Lesson 1.6 — Math is Ours: We make sense of problems, look for patterns, choose representations and tools, make a plan, watch our progress, and shift strategies when needed — together and on our own.

weDo.title: Quick guided checks — one from each lesson
lines: From 1.4: Not every good reason is an equation. Finish this argument: “I recommend buying two jumbo boxes because …”
From 1.6: When we do math, sometimes we get stuck. What can we try?

youDo.title: Show you're caught up
lines: The practice below mixes problems from Lessons 1.4–1.6. Each problem is tagged with its lesson number.
Stuck on one lesson's problems? Open that lesson from the curriculum menu for the full re-teach.

explore.label: Where does each move belong in the problem-solving process? Sort them.
categories: Making sense and planning (before you're stuck)

cards.text: Think about what you know and don't know about the problem
Look for patterns and relationships among quantities
Visualize the problem and choose a useful representation
Think of questions to ask a classmate or the teacher
Draw pictures of the problem to see it differently
Think of problems you have seen like this before
Identify what you don't understand about the problem

explore.instructions: Both columns are real math. The left column is how a solution starts; the right column is how a stalled solution gets moving again. After sorting, star the get-unstuck move you will actually try next time.

diagram.title: 6 Times as Many Wheels
diagram.caption: One group's 3 wheels is a single unit; six copies of that unit make 18 wheels, so "6 times as many" means 6 × 3, not 6 + 3.

connect.scenario: Communities often have agreements that all members agree to in order to be part of the community. Our math class is a community of thinkers and doers — when we work together we listen attentively, share our thinking, respect others' ideas, critique ideas (not classmates), and take turns. When we work alone we stay focused, seek help when stuck, and respect classmates' boundaries.
connect.promptQuestion: What ideas do you recommend that the whole class agrees to so that math class is a community of learners?
connect.prompt: Propose a class agreement for working ___, and another for working alone, based on showing ___ for classmates. State each idea as a clear class ___ that helps everyone learn.

check.stem: Which is an example of a working-together agreement that supports the class as a community of thinkers?
choices: Only share ideas when you're sure they're correct
Critique the ideas that are shared, not the classmates who shared them
Let the fastest student finish problems for the group
Work silently so no one is distracted
check.explanation: Separating critique of ideas from criticism of people keeps it safe to share half-formed thinking, which is where good math starts. Requiring certainty before sharing discourages participation, letting one student finish for the group excludes others, and working silently describes working alone, not together.

check.stem: Which is an example of a working-alone agreement that still supports the whole class?
choices: Never ask for help, even when stuck
Interrupt a classmate anytime you have a question
Seek help when stuck, without interrupting classmates unnecessarily
Skip any problem you find difficult
check.explanation: Seeking help without unnecessary interruptions lets a student get unstuck while still respecting classmates' focus and boundaries. Never asking for help leaves a student stuck, interrupting freely ignores classmates' boundaries, and skipping hard problems avoids the productive struggle math class asks for.

check.stem: Why should the class agree on both a together-agreement and an alone-agreement?
choices: Because working alone matters more than working together
Because math class includes both kinds of work, and each kind needs its own way to support the whole community
Because agreements for working together are only for advanced students
Because agreements about working alone don't affect other students
check.explanation: The class works together sometimes and alone sometimes, so agreements are needed for both to keep the whole community supported. Neither kind of work matters 'more,' agreements aren't limited by ability level, and alone-work choices like interrupting or seeking help do affect classmates.

connect.modelAnswer: For working together, I propose: we critique the ideas of others, not our classmates — so everyone feels safe sharing a half-formed idea, which is where good math starts. For working on our own, I propose: we seek help when we are stuck, but avoid interrupting classmates unnecessarily — so nobody stays stuck for a whole class, and nobody loses their focus either.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 1.4) An egg muffin is about 60 calories. A plate holds 4 egg muffins. About how many calories are on the plate?
choices: About 240
About 64
About 15
About 600
approaching.explanation: 4 muffins at about 60 calories each is 60 × 4 = 240 calories.
choiceFeedback: That adds 60 + 4 instead of multiplying.
That divides 60 by 4 instead of multiplying.
That multiplies 60 by 10 instead of by 4.
hints: How many muffins, and how many calories in each one?
4 equal groups of 60.
Multiply 60 × 4.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 1.4) A large cereal box is 8 in long, 3 in wide, and 10 in tall. What is its volume?
choices: 240 cubic inches
21 cubic inches
80 cubic inches
240 square inches
approaching.explanation: Volume of a rectangular prism is length × width × height: 8 × 3 × 10 = 240 cubic inches.
choiceFeedback: That adds 8 + 3 + 10 instead of multiplying the dimensions.
That multiplies only 8 × 10 and leaves out the 3-inch width.
The number is right, but volume is measured in CUBIC inches — square inches measure area.
hints: Volume of a box is length × width × height.
Multiply 8 × 3 first, then use the height.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 1.5) Each penny has a value of $0.01. What is the value of 100 pennies?
approaching.explanation: 100 × $0.01 = $1.00 — one hundred hundredths make one whole dollar.
choiceFeedback: $0.10 is the value of only 10 pennies, not 100.
$10.00 is the value of 100 DIMES — that uses the wrong coin's value.
$100.00 treats each penny as a dollar instead of a hundredth of a dollar.
hints: A penny is one hundredth of a dollar.
How many hundredths make a whole?

approaching.stem: (Lesson 1.5) Each quarter has a value of $0.25. Following the pattern, what is the value of 100 quarters?
approaching.explanation: 100 × $0.25 = $25.00 — the same pattern as 100 pennies making $1.00 and 100 nickels making $5.00.
choiceFeedback: $2.50 is the value of only 10 quarters — that multiplies by 10 instead of 100.
$250.00 multiplies by 1,000 instead of 100.
$100.25 adds 100 + 0.25 instead of multiplying.
hints: Multiplying by 100 moves the decimal point.
100 pennies → $1.00, 100 dimes → $10. Same move.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 1.6) A bicycle rack holds 8 bikes, and each bike has 2 wheels. How many wheels are on the rack?
approaching.explanation: 8 bikes with 2 wheels each is 8 × 2 = 16 wheels.
choiceFeedback: That adds 8 + 2 instead of multiplying.
That divides 8 by 2 instead of multiplying.
That places the digits 8 and 2 side by side instead of multiplying them.
hints: How many groups, and how many wheels in each group?
8 groups of 2.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 1.6) Another bicycle rack has 6 times as many wheels as the rack with 16 wheels. About how many wheels does it have?
choices: About 96
About 22
About 66
About 616
approaching.explanation: 6 times as many as 16 is 16 × 6 = 96 wheels.
choiceFeedback: That adds 16 + 6 instead of multiplying — '6 times as many' means multiply.
That multiplies 6 by 11, or misreads '6 times' as 'some sixes' — the answer must be 6 groups of 16.
That places 6 and 16 side by side instead of multiplying them.
hints: '6 times as many' tells you the operation.
6 groups of 16.

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 1.4) Three large boxes hold 240 cubic inches each. Two jumbo boxes hold 400 cubic inches each. Which is the correct volume comparison?
choices: 720 cubic inches vs. 800 cubic inches — the jumbo option holds more
720 cubic inches vs. 800 cubic inches — the large option holds more
240 cubic inches vs. 400 cubic inches — the jumbo option holds more
480 cubic inches vs. 800 cubic inches — the jumbo option holds more
onLevel.explanation: 240 × 3 = 720 and 400 × 2 = 800; since 800 > 720, the two jumbo boxes hold more in total.
choiceFeedback: The totals are right, but 800 is GREATER than 720, so the jumbo option wins the comparison.
That compares one box of each size instead of the full purchase — three larges vs. two jumbos.
480 comes from 240 × 2 — the large option has THREE boxes, not two.
hints: Find each TOTAL before comparing.
Which total is greater?

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 1.4) One garden bed is 4 ft long, 3 ft wide, and 2 ft deep. A second bed is 6 ft long, 2 ft wide, and 2 ft deep. How much soil fills BOTH beds?
choices: 48 cubic feet
24 cubic feet
19 cubic feet
96 cubic feet
onLevel.explanation: First bed: 4 × 3 × 2 = 24 cubic feet. Second bed: 6 × 2 × 2 = 24 cubic feet. Together: 24 + 24 = 48 cubic feet.
choiceFeedback: 24 cubic feet is only ONE bed — the problem asks for both.
That adds all the dimensions (4+3+2+6+2+2) instead of multiplying within each bed.
That multiplies the two bed volumes (24 × ... ) too far — you ADD the volumes of the parts, you don't double the total.
hints: Find each bed's volume separately, then combine.
Add the two volumes.

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 1.5) Player A had 18 points before making 10 two-pointers in a row. How many points does Player A have after the streak?
onLevel.explanation: Ten two-pointers add 10 × 2 = 20 points, and 18 + 20 = 38 points.
choiceFeedback: That adds 10 (the number of shots) instead of 20 (the points they are worth).
20 is only the streak's points — it drops the 18 Player A started with.
That adds 30, using Player B's three-point rule on Player A's shots.
hints: The pattern rule for Player A is to add 2, ten times.
Start from 18 and add.

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 1.5) Akela's jar totals $53.50. Why can the number of pennies only be a multiple of 5?
choices: Because the total's cents end in 0, and only pennies make amounts that aren't multiples of 5 cents
Because pennies always come in rolls of 5
Because there are exactly 5 kinds of coins in the jar
Because $53.50 is divisible by 5
onLevel.explanation: Nickels, dimes, and quarters are each worth a multiple of 5 cents. For the total to land on a 0, the pennies must also add up to a multiple of 5 cents — so their count is a multiple of 5.
choiceFeedback: How pennies are packaged has nothing to do with the arithmetic of the total.
The jar holds 4 kinds of coins, and the count of kinds is not the reason anyway.
The total being divisible by 5 is close, but the real reason is that every OTHER coin is already a multiple of 5 cents, so the pennies must be too.
hints: What are nickels, dimes, and quarters each worth in cents?
5, 10, and 25 — all multiples of 5.
So what must the pennies' total be for everything to end in 0?

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 1.6) You are solving a problem and realize your strategy is not making progress. What does the problem-solving process say to do?
choices: Notice your progress has stalled and shift to a different strategy
Keep using the same strategy no matter what
Erase everything and decide the problem is impossible
Copy a classmate's paper
onLevel.explanation: We are aware of our progress in solving the problem and shift strategies when needed.
choiceFeedback: Persistence is good, but the process says to WATCH your progress — repeating a stalled strategy is not persistence.
Your sense-making so far still counts — shifting strategies keeps that work; erasing throws it away.
Copying skips the doing entirely — asking your classmate a QUESTION is the community move.
hints: The process includes watching something while you work.
You stay aware of your progress.
Stalled progress is the signal to shift.

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 1.6) The first rack has 16 wheels and the other rack has 6 times as many. How many BIKES does the bigger rack hold, if every bike has 2 wheels?
onLevel.explanation: The bigger rack has 16 × 6 = 96 wheels, and 96 ÷ 2 = 48 bikes.
choiceFeedback: 96 is the number of WHEELS — the question asks for bikes, so divide by 2.
24 divides 48 by 2 a second time — the wheels only need halving once.
192 multiplies 96 by 2 instead of dividing — more wheels than bikes, not fewer.
hints: First find the wheels, then turn wheels into bikes.
16 × 6 = 96 wheels.
Every bike accounts for 2 of them.

extending.stem: (Lesson 1.4) A student claims: “Greater box volume ALWAYS means more cereal inside.” Which is the best counterexample?
choices: A jumbo box with more volume that is sold half-filled with air
A large box that costs more than a jumbo box
Two jumbo boxes that are easier to store than three large boxes
A box of a different cereal brand
extending.explanation: A counterexample must break the claim itself: a bigger box holding less cereal (more air) shows greater volume does not guarantee more cereal.
choiceFeedback: Price does not test the claim — the claim links volume to AMOUNT of cereal, not cost.
Storage convenience is a different argument entirely; it says nothing about how much cereal is inside.
Changing the brand changes the product, but does not show a bigger box holding less cereal.
hints: A counterexample must make the claim FALSE in one case.
The claim connects volume to amount of cereal.
Find the case where volume is bigger but cereal is not.

extending.stem: (Lesson 1.5) If both players kept their streaks going, after how many MORE shots would Player B tie Player A?
choices: 2 more shots
1 more shot
They can never tie
10 more shots
extending.explanation: The gap is 38 − 36 = 2 and shrinks by 1 each shot (3 − 2 = 1). After 2 more shots: Player A has 38 + 4 = 42 and Player B has 36 + 6 = 42.
choiceFeedback: After 1 shot the scores are 40 and 39 — still 1 apart.
The gap shrinks by 1 every shot, so it must reach 0.
After 10 more shots Player A would have 38 + 20 = 58 and Player B would have 36 + 30 = 66 — Player B would be 8 points ahead, far past a tie.
hints: How big is the gap now, and how much does it change per shot?
Gap of 2, shrinking by 3 − 2 = 1 each shot.
How many shots to close a gap of 2?

extending.stem: (Lesson 1.6) A group solves a hard problem, but one student did all the talking while three stayed silent. By this lesson's standards, how did the GROUP do?
choices: Not well — a community shares thinking and takes turns, so three voices went unheard
Perfectly — the answer was right, and that is all that matters
Not well — the talker should have stayed silent too
Perfectly — silent members were being respectful
extending.explanation: We share our thinking and take turns when sharing ideas — a right answer that silences three thinkers costs the community three sets of ideas.
choiceFeedback: The answer is only half the outcome — the community also has to grow, and three members never shared their thinking.
The talker sharing ideas is good — the miss was not making room for the other three, not the talking itself.
Respect includes sharing YOUR thinking too — the agreements ask for turn-taking, not silence.
hints: What do the working-together agreements say about sharing?
We share our thinking and take turns.
Did all four members get to do that?

practice.commonMistake: Treating 'stuck' as a stop sign instead of a signal — waiting silently instead of trying a strategy: asking a question, drawing the problem, or recalling a similar problem.

optionalActivity.name: Catch-Up Challenge
optionalActivity.intro: Mix it up: pick the right lesson's big idea for each problem — that's the real catch-up skill.

exitTicket.stem: (Catch-up check, from Lesson 1.5) Which statement best captures what this lesson means by 'Math is Finding Patterns'?
choices: We look for patterns and relationships, use them to solve problems and make generalizations, and check our solutions for reasonableness
Patterns are decorations that make problems look nicer
A pattern rule only works if you also count every item one at a time
Once you spot a pattern you never need to check your answer
exitTicket.explanation: The summary lists exactly this: we look for patterns and relationships, use them to solve problems, notice repeated calculations to make generalizations, and evaluate the reasonableness of our solutions as we work.
hints: Look back at the Summarize slide.
It has four parts: notice, use, generalize, check.
Which option keeps all four?

steps.promptEs: 6 cabe en 252 aproximadamente ___ veces.

steps.prompt: Multiply back: 6 × 42 = ___.
steps.promptEs: Multiplica para comprobar: 6 × 42 = ___.

steps.prompt: The amount left is ___.
steps.promptEs: La cantidad que sobra es ___.

hints: Re-read the question. What exactly is it asking you to find?
Use the visual model, then complete one step at a time.
Start like this: 6 fits into 252 about 42 times.
